clue.text: Freebooter shows how to deal with a cigar!

wordplay.words: how to deal with a cigar
wordplay.note: a cigar is dressed with a paper band

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a pirate is an expert on how to treat a cigar.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase reads as an instruction, BAND IT: cigars wear a paper band round them.
explanation.definitionFit: A freebooter is a pirate or plundering adventurer, and a bandit is a robber of the same lawless kind.

clue.text: Two-master's unaspirated crew are toughies!

indicators.note: aspiration is the breathy h sound, so unaspirated means that letter is dropped

parts.note: a brig is a two-masted sailing ship
a ship's crew are its hands

explanation.surface: The crew of a two-masted ship, dropping their aitches, are a rough lot.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the h at the start of a word, as in a Cockney accent, is what 'unaspirated' describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigands are armed robbers living outside the law, the kind of hard men loosely called toughies.

clue.text: Master of the Rolls in Ancient Rome?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: the senior English judge called Master of the Rolls, oddly placed in Rome
setter's reading: a Roman servant who mastered the roll of names, prompting his master with the names of people he met

explanation.surface: Imagining a Roman equivalent of the English judge called the Master of the Rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: The Master of the Rolls is a senior English judge; here the 'rolls' are lists of names a Roman slave had to know by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nomenclator was a slave whose job was to remember and announce people's names, a living roll of citizens.

clue.text: It's but a trifle in reckoning agiotage

indicators.note: the answer sits inside a longer clue word, so 'in' points us within it

parts.note: the letters run consecutively inside this word for currency-exchange dealing

explanation.surface: Remarking that the profit in currency speculation counts for very little.
explanation.walkthrough: Agiotage is the business of money-changing or speculating on exchange rates.
explanation.definitionFit: An iota is the smallest Greek letter and so stands for a very small amount, a mere jot.

clue.text: Drawing by a volunteer worker in the studio

definitions.note: the answer describes drawing done without instruments, so it works as an adjective or adverb here

parts.note: a volunteer works free, unpaid
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A sketch made by someone helping out unpaid at an artist's studio.
explanation.definitionFit: Freehand drawing is done by eye, without rulers, compasses or tracing to guide the pencil.

clue.text: Animalcules decay provided time is allowed

parts.note: to decay is to rot
provided that means if
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: Tiny creatures will decompose if given enough time.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotifers are microscopic aquatic organisms, the wheel animalcules of older natural history.

clue.text: Displayed by the nose of the Dong?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: something a nose shows, like a sniff or a colour
setter's reading: Edward Lear's poem 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose', whose nose glows brightly in the dark

explanation.surface: Asking what a creature's nose shows off.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dong is the hero of Edward Lear's nonsense poem 'The Dong with a Luminous Nose', which lights up the night.
explanation.definitionFit: Effulgence is a radiant brilliance or glow, exactly what a luminous nose would give off.

clue.text: A thousand and one for a foreign chum

parts.note: taken as written
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Echoes the Thousand and One Nights, as a tale told for a friend abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Ami is the French word for a friend, so it is a pal in a foreign language.

clue.text: Make short work of a meal

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to condense a text into a summary

definitions.note: the verb sense: to process a meal in the stomach
definitions.meaning: second meaning: to break down food after eating it

explanation.surface: Wolfing down a meal quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make short work of' reads as one idiom for eating fast, but the clue splits after 'work'.
explanation.definitionFit: To digest is both to abridge writing into a shorter summary and to break down eaten food in the gut.

clue.text: Stage confidence

parts.note: surface reading: an actor's self-assurance before an audience; setter's reading: a secret confided, here one spoken on a stage for the audience but supposedly unheard by other characters

explanation.walkthrough: Confidence means self-assurance in the surface, but a shared secret in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In theatre, an actor's remark addressed to the audience and unheard by others on stage is a secret confided to them.

clue.text: Fractured main leads to setback for lodgers

parts.note: the four letters rearranged

indicators.note: the back half of this word says to put the front half back to front
something fractured is broken into pieces, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the first three letters, set, taken as written and then turned round by the rest of the word

explanation.surface: A burst water main causes trouble for people renting rooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setback' looks like one word meaning a reverse, but splits into SET and its reversal indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Inmates are those who share a house or institution as residents, an old sense close to lodgers.

clue.text: Upholstery work for titled undergraduates?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: securing padding with tufts of thread through the cover

definitions.note: a jokey sense: hunting for or courting tufts
definitions.meaning: second meaning: tufts were titled undergraduates at Oxford and Cambridge, so going after them is a whimsical sense

explanation.surface: Imagining aristocratic students doing upholstery.
explanation.walkthrough: At old Oxford and Cambridge, a 'tuft' was a nobleman undergraduate, named for the gold tassel on his cap; 'tuft-hunting' was toadying to them.
explanation.definitionFit: Tufting is the upholsterer's technique of pulling cushions in with buttoned tufts, and also courting titled students.

clue.text: Swan takes a turn amid the crops

definitions.note: describes things found among cereal crops

indicators.note: taking a turn suggests moving about, so the letters change position

parts.note: the four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A swan wanders around among farm fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Awns are the stiff bristles on the ears of barley, wheat and other grain crops.

clue.text: Benevolent orramen?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: kindly, charitable people
setter's reading: orra is Scots for odd, and orramen are odd-job men, so they are odd men, the name of a friendly society

explanation.walkthrough: Orraman is a Scots word for an odd-job labourer; taken literally, orra men are odd men.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oddfellows are a long-established friendly society providing mutual aid and charitable benefits to members.

clue.text: Oily peace — feeler

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a smooth, unctuous diplomat; setter's reading: coming from the tree that yields oil
setter's reading: a feeler is a shoot put out, and the shoot of that oil tree is the classic peace offering

explanation.surface: A slick, insincere overture towards making peace.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits 'peace-feeler'; a feeler is both a tentative approach and a branch reaching out.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig from the oil-bearing tree has been a symbol of peace since the dove returned to Noah's ark.

clue.text: A minimum tied up in overheads or over-foot?

definitions.text: A minimum tied up in overheads
definitions.meaning: surface reading: a small budget swallowed up by business running costs
setter's reading: a lace tied over the foot, which also means running something on a tiny budget

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a scant budget goes on running costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overheads' are business costs; 'over-foot' is the setter's coinage for where a lace is tied.
explanation.definitionFit: Running a business on a lace-thin budget means the bare minimum of money, and the lace itself is tied over the foot.

clue.text: Here I'd help to produce an oracle

definitions.text: Here I'd help to produce an oracle

indicators.note: producing means making something new out of material, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A priestess saying this is where she helps deliver prophecies.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: 'here' is the place where the speaker helped to give out oracles.
explanation.definitionFit: Delphi in ancient Greece was the shrine of Apollo, where the Pythia priestess delivered prophecies to visitors.

clue.text: Mister A in classical disguise

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so the letters appear in a new form

parts.note: the seven letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A man disguised in Greek costume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classical' does double duty, pointing to Greek myth for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Artemis is the classical Greek goddess of the hunt and moon, a mythological figure from antiquity.

clue.text: A cry in the night with a happy ending

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the call of a night watchman reporting no trouble

definitions.note: a play title shortened, not a phrase of the same grammar
definitions.meaning: second meaning: Shakespeare's comedy '... That Ends Well'

explanation.surface: A nighttime scream that turns out fine in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half alludes to Shakespeare's 'All's Well That Ends Well'.
explanation.definitionFit: Watchmen once called out that everything was safe on their rounds, and Shakespeare's comedy title promises a fortunate conclusion.

clue.text: Payments here for the cloth

parts.note: surface reading: money paid for fabric, as at a draper's; setter's reading: the cloth means the clergy, so these are clergymen's salaries

explanation.walkthrough: 'The cloth' is a traditional term for the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is the fixed salary paid to a minister of the church, the usual word for clerical pay.

clue.text: Turn to greet a swarthy hero

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the opposite way

parts.note: the little word taken as written
you greet someone with hello

explanation.surface: Instructions to turn round and welcome a dark-skinned champion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' looks like a link word, but it is the piece being turned.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello, Shakespeare's Moor of Venice, is the play's tragic protagonist, described as dark-skinned.

clue.text: The mark of stress?

parts.note: surface reading: a sign of strain or anxiety in a person; setter's reading: stress as emphasis on a syllable, and the written mark placed over it

explanation.walkthrough: Stress is first read as worry, but in phonetics it is emphasis on a syllable.
explanation.definitionFit: An acute or grave sign written over a vowel marks where emphasis falls in pronunciation.

clue.text: Plebeian pudding

parts.note: surface reading: a humble, common dessert; setter's reading: the word for dessert itself is the common one, considered non-U by the class-conscious

explanation.walkthrough: In mid-century Britain, word choice marked class; the posh said 'pudding' and others used a different word.
explanation.definitionFit: Afters is the informal British word for the sweet course that comes after the main dish.

clue.text: "For the rain it raineth every day", he sang

definitions.text: "For the rain it raineth every day"
definitions.meaning: surface reading: a gloomy line about the weather
setter's reading: the singer is the clown in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, whose closing song has this refrain

explanation.walkthrough: The line is the refrain of the song that ends Shakespeare's Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: Feste, Olivia's jester in Twelfth Night, closes the play with the song 'When that I was and a little tiny boy'.

clue.text: Anticipations of a softer seat

indicators.note: a weak signal: the letters are made out of, that is formed from, the words that follow

parts.note: the ten letters of softer seat rearranged; the a is ignored

explanation.surface: Looking forward to a more comfortable chair.
explanation.definitionFit: Foretastes are early samples or previews of what is to come, so they amount to expectations.

clue.text: Clutch of a raven

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a firm hold
second meaning: the pet raven in Dickens's Barnaby Rudge

explanation.surface: A raven's talons clutching their prey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clutch' also suggests a set of eggs, which suits a bird, but here it is a hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip is a tight clasp, and Grip is the talking raven belonging to Barnaby in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Monumental girl in the park

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a huge or impressive young woman
setter's reading: a memorial sculpture by Jacob Epstein in London's Hyde Park depicting the heroine of Green Mansions

explanation.walkthrough: Epstein's carving in Hyde Park, a large London park, honours W. H. Hudson and depicts the bird-girl heroine of his novel Green Mansions.
explanation.definitionFit: Rima is the forest girl of Hudson's novel, commemorated in a famous Epstein relief in a London park.

clue.text: "Like nature's patient sleepless -" (Keats)

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a line with a word missing for the solver to complete
setter's reading: the line comes from his sonnet 'Bright star', where the star watches like a hermit

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Keats's sonnet 'Bright star, would I were steadfast as thou art'.
explanation.definitionFit: An eremite is a religious hermit, which Keats imagines keeping a lonely all-night vigil like the star.

clue.text: Organ frequently on loan

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a church instrument or a body part lent out
setter's reading: people often 'lend' this body part when they listen

explanation.walkthrough: Mark Antony's 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears' is the idiom behind the loan.
explanation.definitionFit: This hearing organ is what a listener gives someone when paying attention, so it is idiomatically lent.

clue.text: Three nameless in a palace

parts.note: tri- is the prefix meaning three
anon is short for anonymous

explanation.surface: Three unknown people inside a royal residence.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grand and Petit Trianon are two smaller royal residences in the grounds of Versailles.

clue.text: "Say not the — naught availeth". (Clough)

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a quotation with a gap to complete
setter's reading: Arthur Hugh Clough's poem opens with this line, a call not to give up the fight

explanation.walkthrough: The line opens Clough's poem, famously quoted by Churchill in 1941.
explanation.definitionFit: Clough's poem urges that effortful fighting is never in vain, and the missing noun names that effort.

clue.text: For graduate to approach Tom is an anticlimax

parts.note: a Bachelor of Arts is a graduate
Thos is the old written abbreviation of Thomas, Tom's full name

explanation.surface: A graduate chatting up a man called Tom ends in disappointment.
explanation.definitionFit: Bathos is a sudden comic drop from the elevated to the trivial, the literary letdown of an anticlimax.
